strengths: The paper addresses an important question: how adversarial training can preserve clean generalization while exhibiting a large robust generalization gap. Separating representation complexity from training dynamics provides a useful organizing framework.

The proposed mechanism—partial learning of shared signal combined with memorization of sample-specific noise—is intuitive and worth investigating. Combining a memorization construction with nonlinear feature-learning analysis is well motivated.

The experiments report clean test, robust training, and robust test accuracy separately. Synthetic feature trajectories and the additional loss-landscape diagnostics provide useful qualitative illustrations.
weaknesses: Theorem 4.4 is false under its stated assumptions. Consider equal probability on two inputs ±e1/2, with corresponding labels ±1, radius δ=1/4, and clean classifier f(x)=x1−0.4. This satisfies Assumptions 4.1–4.3: clean error is zero and robust error is 1/2. With a growing sample, both atoms occur at nonvanishing frequencies, so vanishing robust training error forces zero robust population error. Consequently, no CGRO classifier exists in this example. Additional distributional and sample-size conditions are essential.

The representation construction also contains independent proof gaps. Assumption 4.2 separates opposite classes; it does not imply that all training-point perturbation balls are disjoint, as asserted on page 4. The subsequent replacement of a union indicator by a sum is therefore invalid. Appendix F additionally claims uniform o(1) approximation of a generally discontinuous classifier by continuous ReLU networks. This requires a different construction and an explicit argument controlling classification margins and transition regions.

The clean-generalization argument for Theorem 5.9 is unsound. On page 25, the proof treats a sum of cubic Gaussian projections as sub-Gaussian and uses a corresponding exponential tail bound. A nonzero Gaussian cubic is not sub-Gaussian, and projections across filters share the same test noise. The inference from aggregate memorization V_i=Θ(1) to individual noise-weight norms ||β_r||=Θ(1) is also unjustified. These steps directly support the principal test-error conclusion.

There is a consequential threat-model mismatch. Section 5 restricts training perturbations to the signal direction in the signal patch, leaving memorized noise unchanged. Vanishing loss against this restricted attack does not establish vanishing robust training error over the full norm ball in Definition 3.3. Although a restricted attack can establish a lower bound on full-ball test error, it cannot establish the corresponding upper bound on training error. Thus the stated CGRO conclusion is not proved under a common threat model.

The synthetic validation uses α=δ=10, contradicting the theoretical requirement δ<α. This attack can erase the entire label-bearing signal, making poor robust population performance unavoidable even for an ideal learner. It therefore does not validate the proposed failure mechanism in the intended robustly learnable regime. The image experiments remain largely descriptive: small-model collapse can reflect optimization failure, and local loss flatness does not uniquely identify the proposed memorization construction. Missing PGD step counts, step sizes, restarts, and variability across runs also limit reproducibility.

The originality and explanatory reach of the lower bound need clearer justification. Theorem 4.7 is existential, and an existing linearly separable hard distribution already satisfies the broader polynomial-size-clean-classifier condition. Appendix F again uses a locally linear construction, so the claimed extension over Li et al. (2022) is unclear. Moreover, this worst-case result does not establish a representation barrier for the structured distribution analyzed in Section 5 or the experimental datasets.

The additional global-flatness bound in Theorem B.1 is also unsupported as stated. A constant classifier has zero input-gradient flatness, yet its empirical and population losses can differ because sampled label proportions fluctuate. The theorem would incorrectly eliminate this generalization fluctuation. Appendix G does not justify removing the KDE bias and variance terms or obtaining the stated sample-size rate for a fixed attack radius.
